Agree a two-minute review with two questions only: what actually happened, and what would a kind observer say. Then a physical switch. Practice on the last event the client replayed.

fields.label: The event I keep replaying
What I replay most (a sentence, a look, a pause)
My two-minute review: what actually happened
What a kind observer would say
My switch when the two minutes are up
How long the replay used to last, and how long it lasted this time

title: Social Prediction Log
summary: Records the client's forecast before a social situation and the outcome after, to compare over weeks.
goal: Build the client's own evidence that their predictions run far worse than events.
body_md: The forecast must be specific and rated: they will notice me blushing and think less of me, seventy percent. Afterward the client records what observably happened, not how it felt. Review the gap across ten entries, which is usually where belief shifts rather than in any single event.

fields.label: The upcoming situation
What I predict will happen, specifically
How sure I am (0-100%)
What observably happened
How I know (what people said or did)
How the prediction compared
What I predict next time, adjusted

title: Conversation Toolkit Card
summary: A pocket card of openers, follow-up questions and graceful exits for social situations.
goal: Reduce the load of inventing conversation so the client can practice being in it.
body_md: Build it with the client's own words, not scripts from a book, and include exits, since knowing they can leave makes staying easier. Warn against using it as a safety behavior: the card is for learning, and the goal is to need it less. Rehearse a full opener-question-exit in session.

fields.label: Three openers I could actually say
Three follow-up questions that work in most conversations
Two ways to leave a conversation gracefully
What I will do with my hands
The one I will try first this week
How it went, and whether I needed the card

title: Social Brave Steps for Teens
summary: A teen's own ladder of social situations from easy to hard, with a brave step per week.
goal: Give a teenager a graded, self-chosen path back into the social situations they have been dodging.
body_md: Let the teen build and order the steps; a ladder chosen by an adult will not be climbed. Keep parents to a support role agreed on the sheet. Steps should be specific: ask one question in class, not participate more. Celebrate attempts, not outcomes, and expect a step to be repeated before moving up.

fields.label: Situations I have been avoiding
My ladder, easiest at the bottom
This week's step
What I am afraid will happen
What actually happened
What my parent will do (and not do) to help
The step for next week

title: Continuing Bonds Letter
summary: A letter to the person who died, about what has happened since and what the client still carries of them.
goal: Support an ongoing connection with the person rather than a closing of the door.
body_md: Offer it as one option among several, since some clients find writing to the dead unbearable and others find it the only thing that helps. Frame the bond as something that changes rather than ends. The client decides whether to read it aloud, keep it, or take it somewhere. Include 988 among the prompts for the darkest hours.

fields.label: What I want to tell you about since you died
What I have kept of you (a habit, a phrase, an object, a way of seeing)
What I wish I had said
What I think you would say to me now
How I will keep you in my life going forward
If the grief ever gets dangerously dark: 988 (call or text), and who else I will reach

title: Grief Triggers Calendar
summary: A year at a glance with the dates, seasons and events likely to bring the grief up hard.
goal: Let the client see the hard days coming and plan support for them instead of being ambushed.
body_md: Include the obvious dates and the sideways ones: the first snow, the tax season the person used to handle, the song at the store. Plan for the week before an anniversary, which is often worse than the day. Decide with the client who will know about each date.

fields.label: Anniversaries and birthdays
Seasons, holidays and rituals that will be different
Sideways reminders I can predict
The next hard date, and what I will do that day
Who will know it is coming
What helped on the last hard date, and what did not

title: Dual Process Week Planner
summary: A week planned with time for facing the loss and time for the ordinary business of living, both on purpose.
goal: Normalize moving between grief and daily life instead of feeling guilty about either.
body_md: Explain that healthy grief moves between the loss and the rest of life, and that neither side is avoidance. Clients stuck on one side feel guilty when they laugh, or numb when they cannot cry; the planner gives both permission. Keep the entries small and concrete.

fields.label: Times this week I will let myself be with the loss (looking at photos, visiting, talking about them)
Times this week I will do ordinary or even pleasant things
The side I tend to get stuck on
What guilt says when I switch sides
What I will say back to it
How the week went

title: Memory Box Project
summary: A child decorates a box and fills it with objects, drawings and stories that hold the person who died.
goal: Give a grieving child a concrete, permitted place for their memories and a way to talk about them.
body_md: Let the child lead on what goes in and what stays private. Each item comes with a story the child tells if they want to; the telling is the work. Involve the surviving parent or carer where possible, and coach them to follow the child's pace rather than their own. Revisit the box on hard dates.

fields.label: What my box looks like
The first three things I put in it, and why
A story that goes with one of them
Something I want to ask about the person who died
Who I can open the box with
When I might want to open it

title: Grief Conversation Cards
summary: A deck of gentle prompts about the person who died, drawn in turn by family members or a group.
goal: Let a family or group talk about the person in a structured, low-pressure way.
body_md: Write the prompts with the group first so nothing on a card ambushes anyone, mixing light ones with heavier ones. Any card can be passed. Play in a circle with a talking object. In families, children often answer more freely than adults, which gives the adults permission.

fields.label: Prompts we put on the cards
The card I drew, and what I said
Something I learned about the person from someone else
A card I passed on
The card I would like to answer next time

title: Needs Inventory for Partners
summary: Each partner lists their needs in the relationship, ranked, and guesses their partner's list before comparing.
goal: Replace assumed needs with stated ones, and show each partner what the other has been guessing.
body_md: Have both partners complete it separately, including the guess about each other, before any discussion. The gaps between the guess and the real list are the material. Keep the tone of curiosity when a partner's need surprises the other; surprise is information, not an accusation.

fields.label: My top five needs in this relationship, ranked
How well each is being met right now (0-10)
What I think my partner's top five are
What surprised me about their real list
One need of theirs I could meet better this month
One need of mine I will ask for directly

title: Perpetual Problems Sorter
summary: Sorts a couple's recurring arguments into the solvable and the perpetual, and plans a different approach to each.
goal: Stop a couple from trying to solve what needs managing, and from managing what could be solved.
body_md: List the arguments first, then sort. Perpetual problems come from differences in personality or values and will be there in ten years; the goal is dialogue and humor about them, not a fix. Solvable problems get a concrete plan. Most couples are relieved to hear that having perpetual problems is normal.

fields.label: Arguments we have more than once a month
Which of these come from a difference in who we are
Which could actually be solved with a plan
For one solvable problem: our plan
For one perpetual problem: what we can each accept
How we will talk about the perpetual one next time it comes up

title: Trust Rebuilding Steps
summary: A shared ladder of specific, observable actions that would rebuild trust after a breach, with a timeline.
goal: Turn a vague demand to earn trust back into steps both partners can see happening.
body_md: The hurt partner names what would help; the other partner says what they can commit to. Steps must be observable, since promises to change are not. Agree how long the checking phase lasts, because trust cannot rebuild under permanent surveillance. Review progress monthly in session.

fields.label: What was broken, in one sentence each
Actions that would help me trust again (specific and visible)
Which of these I can commit to, and when
What transparency looks like for now, and for how long
What I need to hear when I have a wobble
How we will mark progress

title: Communication Pattern Replay
summary: Replays one recent exchange line by line, with each partner naming what they meant and what they heard.
goal: Show a couple the gap between what was said, what was meant and what landed.
body_md: Pick a short exchange, not the biggest fight. Write the actual lines, then have each partner add what they meant and what they heard. The gaps are usually where the fight lives. Finish by rewriting two lines each, and rehearse the rewrite in session.

fields.label: The exchange, line by line, as it happened
For my lines: what I meant
For their lines: what I heard
Where the gap between meant and heard was widest
Two lines I would rewrite
How the rewritten version sounds out loud

title: Relationship Values Compass
summary: Each partner names the kind of partner they want to be, separately from how the other is behaving.
goal: Anchor each partner to their own values so change does not wait on the other person moving first.
body_md: Works with a couple or with one partner alone. The key move is separating my values as a partner from what I get back; clients often discover they have been acting on a scoreboard. Choose one valued action for the week that does not depend on the other person's response.

fields.label: The partner I want to be, in three words
How I have actually been acting lately
What I have been waiting for my partner to do first
One valued action I will take this week regardless
What my mind says will happen if I go first
What actually happened

title: Safety and Stabilization Plan
summary: A plan for the practical and emotional safety a survivor needs in place before any deeper work.
goal: Put steady ground under the client first: who, where, what, and what to do when it gets too much.
body_md: Complete it together in session and never as homework. Cover present-day safety from the person who harmed them, the people who help, the skills that bring them back, and what to do in the worst hours. Move at the client's pace and do not ask for the details of what happened; that is not what this sheet is for. Include 988.

fields.label: Am I safe from the person now? What would make me safer
People I trust, and what each one can help with
Skills that bring me back when I am flooded
Signs that I am doing too much too fast
What I will do in the worst hour: 988 (call or text), and my other numbers
What I want my therapist to know about pace
What I am not ready to talk about yet, and that is fine

title: Consent and Boundaries Map
summary: Maps the client's yes, no and maybe across touch, closeness and conversation, in their own words.
goal: Help a survivor reclaim the right to decide, in small everyday ways, what they allow and what they do not.
body_md: Keep it to everyday boundaries at first: hugs, sitting close, questions from family, who has their number. The maybe column matters, since survivors often feel boundaries must be absolute to count. Rehearse one no in session. Nothing here asks about the abuse itself.

fields.label: Things I am a clear yes to
Things I am a clear no to
Things that are a maybe, and what would make them a yes
A boundary someone in my life keeps crossing
How I will say no to that, in my words
What I will do if they push
Someone who respects my boundaries well

title: Shame Response Sheet
summary: Catches the self-blame that follows abuse, tests it against what the client would say to another survivor, and writes the fairer version.
goal: Loosen the belief that the client caused, allowed or deserved what happened.
body_md: Do this in session, gently, and expect the double standard to be stark: the client will extend to another survivor a compassion they refuse themselves. Do not argue the client out of the belief; let the comparison do the work, and rate belief before and after. Stop if the client becomes flooded and return to grounding.

fields.label: What I tell myself about why it happened
How much I believe that (0-100%)
What I would say to a friend who told me the same story
Where the blame actually belongs
The fairer statement, in my words
How much I believe the fairer statement now (0-100%)

title: Support Disclosure Planner
summary: Plans whether, who, when and how much to tell, so a disclosure happens on the client's terms.
goal: Keep the choice of who knows, and how much, in the survivor's hands.
body_md: Not telling is a valid outcome of this sheet and should be said out loud. Work through what the client wants from telling, who is likely to respond well, and how much to say; a first sentence and an exit line are worth rehearsing. Plan for the reaction being disappointing, since it sometimes is.

fields.label: What I hope telling someone would give me
People I might tell, and how I think each would respond
The person I would tell first, if anyone
How much I want to say (a sentence is enough)
My first sentence
How I will end the conversation if I need to
What I will do for myself afterward, whatever their reaction

title: Body Safety Rules Poster
summary: A child makes a poster of body safety rules: private parts, okay and not-okay touch, secrets versus surprises, and who to tell.
goal: Teach a child the words and the permission to tell, as part of prevention work with families.
body_md: A prevention and education tool, done with a parent in the room where possible. Use correct names for body parts. Teach that surprises are fun and short and secrets about bodies are never kept. List five trusted adults. If a child discloses during this, stop the activity, stay calm, believe them, and follow your mandated reporting duties.

fields.label: Private parts have proper names, and mine are
Okay touch and not-okay touch: my examples
The difference between a surprise and a secret
My five trusted grown-ups
What I say if someone breaks a body safety rule
Where my poster will hang

title: Coping Menu by Situation
summary: A menu of the client's coping options sorted by where they are: at work, in public, at home, in bed.
goal: Match skills to settings so the right one is available where the distress actually happens.
body_md: Most clients have skills that only work at home and distress that happens elsewhere. Sort by setting and check that each setting has at least two options that are invisible to other people. Include one for the middle of the night. Keep the menu in the phone's notes.

fields.label: At work or school: two things I can do without anyone noticing
In public: two options
At home: two options
In bed at 3 a.m.: two options
The skill I reach for too often, and where it does not work
The new skill I will try this week, and where

title: Skill Practice Log
summary: A weekly log of which coping skill the client used, in what situation, and how well it worked.
goal: Turn coping from a vague resolve into a tracked practice with results.
body_md: The rating is the useful part: a skill that scores three out of ten in three different situations can be retired without guilt. Look for the mismatch between skills tried and situations faced. Praise the attempt, especially when the skill did not work, since trying is what builds the habit.

fields.label: Date and the situation
Distress before (0-10)
The skill I used
Distress after (0-10)
How well it worked (0-10) and why
A skill I could have used instead
The skill I will practice most next week

title: Coping Ladder for Kids
summary: A ladder of a child's coping moves from small feelings at the bottom to big ones at the top.
goal: Match the size of the coping move to the size of the feeling, in a picture a child can use.
body_md: Draw a ladder with three or four rungs and let the child assign feelings sizes to each. Small feelings get small moves: a breath, a drink of water. Big feelings get big moves: a break, a grown-up. Practice one move per rung in session and have the parent post the ladder at home.

fields.label: Bottom rung: a small feeling and my small move
Middle rung: a medium feeling and my medium move
Top rung: a huge feeling and my biggest move
How I know which rung I am on
Who helps me on the top rung
Where my ladder is posted

title: Coping Skills Relay
summary: Teams race to act out or demonstrate a coping skill for each situation card drawn.
goal: Rehearse coping skills under mild pressure and laughter, so they are practiced rather than just known.
body_md: Write situation cards with the group beforehand: a test tomorrow, a friend ignoring a text, a loud house. A team scores when the skill fits the situation and could actually be done there. Judge fit, not speed, and let the group argue the call; the argument is the learning.

fields.label: Situation cards we made
Skills my team demonstrated
A skill another team showed that I want to steal
A situation none of us could match well
The skill I will practice this week

title: Helpful vs Costly Coping Sort
summary: Sorts everything the client does to feel better into what helps in the long run and what costs more than it gives.
goal: Help the client judge coping by its long-term workability rather than by how fast it works.
body_md: List everything without judgment first, including the ones the client is ashamed of; those are usually the fastest-acting. Sort by long-term workability, not by how they look. Most clients find a few things belong in both columns depending on amount, which is worth writing down rather than resolving.

fields.label: Everything I do to feel better, fast or slow
Which ones help me next week too
Which ones cost more than they give
Which ones depend on how much
One costly one I will shrink, and how
One helpful one I will do more of, and when

title: Phobia Prediction Tracker
summary: Records what the client expects to happen around the feared object or situation and what actually occurs.
goal: Build the client's own evidence that the feared outcome and the felt danger diverge.
body_md: Ask for the specific feared outcome, not just fear: I will faint, the dog will bite, the plane will crash. Rate belief before and after each approach. The pattern across entries is what changes belief, so aim for at least eight entries before drawing conclusions together.

fields.label: The feared thing and the situation
What I predict will happen, specifically
How sure I am (0-100%)
Peak fear (0-10)
What actually happened
What I did during the peak
My belief in the prediction now (0-100%)

title: Approach Steps Planner
summary: Plans the next approach step toward a feared object in detail: where, how long, with whom, and what to drop.
goal: Make each approach step concrete enough to actually happen this week.
body_md: One step at a time, planned to the minute. Include what safety moves the client will drop, since carrying the escape plan into the step blunts it. Decide in advance how long to stay: long enough for the fear to fall, not just to touch and run. Debrief in session before planning the next.

fields.label: This week's step
Where and when, exactly
Who will be there, and what they will and will not do
How long I will stay (until fear drops by half)
The safety moves I will not use
What happened, and what I will do next week

title: Phobia Body Response Sheet
summary: Names what the client's body does around the feared thing, and separates the alarm from the danger.
goal: Help the client see the fear response as an alarm that can fire without a fire.
body_md: Map the response: heart, breath, muscles, stomach, the urge to run. Explain plainly that the body's alarm is doing its job and that the job is to get them out, which is why staying feels wrong. For blood or needle fears, note the faint response and plan applied tension separately.

fields.label: What my body does first around the feared thing
What it does next
The urge that comes with it
What the alarm is trying to make me do
What I know about the real danger in this situation
What I will do with the alarm next time it fires

title: Brave Practice Chart for Kids
summary: A sticker chart for a child's repeated brave practices with a feared thing, tied to a small reward.
goal: Make repetition of approach steps visible and rewarding for a child.
duration: 20 minutes to set up, then daily
body_md: Choose practices small enough to repeat daily: look at a picture of a dog, stand in the doorway with the lights off. Stickers go on for attempts, not for calm. Parents hold the chart and the reward and keep their own anxiety out of the practice. Change the practice when it stops earning fear.

fields.label: My brave practice this week
Stickers I earned
How scared I was the first time (0-10) and the last time
My reward when the chart is full
What my grown-up does during practice
Next week's brave practice

title: Fear Ladder Card Sort
summary: Situations written on cards and physically sorted into a ladder from least to most scary.
goal: Build a fear hierarchy as a hands-on sorting task rather than a form.
body_md: Write one situation per card with the client, at least fifteen, then sort them on the table or floor. The physical sorting draws out distinctions a form misses, and the client can move cards as beliefs change. Photograph the finished ladder and use it to choose the next approach step.

fields.label: Situations we wrote on cards
The bottom three cards
The top three cards
Cards I moved while sorting, and why
The card I will start with
The card I cannot imagine reaching yet

title: Body Neutrality Practice
summary: Daily short statements about what the body did today rather than how it looked.
goal: Move the client's relationship with their body from judgment toward function and use.
duration: Two minutes daily for two weeks
body_md: Aim for neutral, not positive; clients who cannot believe their body is beautiful can believe it carried them up the stairs. Keep the statements about doing and feeling. Notice when the client sneaks an appearance comment in and gently redirect. Never mention weight, shape or food in this practice.

fields.label: Three things my body did for me today
One thing it let me feel (warmth, music, a hug, the wind)
A neutral statement about my body, without judgment either way
What my mind wanted to add about how it looks
How I responded to that
The statement I will use tomorrow morning

title: Body Checking Log
summary: Records the mirror checks, pinching, comparing and photo scrutiny that keep body worry alive, and what each one did to mood.
goal: Show the client how checking feeds the worry, and plan a reduction.
body_md: Checking feels like getting information but produces worse mood almost every time; the log makes that visible. Include the quiet forms: reflections in windows, comparing in group photos, clothes tried and discarded. Plan one check to cut in half, not to stop entirely.

fields.label: Date and time
What I checked, and how (mirror, pinch, photo, comparing)
What I was looking for
Mood before and after (0-10)
How long the reassurance lasted, if any
The check I will cut in half next week
What I will do instead in that moment

title: Appearance Assumptions Sheet
summary: Lists the client's rules linking appearance to worth, acceptance or success, and tests each one.
goal: Loosen the beliefs that make appearance carry the whole weight of self-worth.
body_md: Draw out the if-then rules: if I looked different, then people would... Test each against the client's own experience and the people they admire. The goal is to shrink the share of self-worth that appearance holds, which a pie chart of what makes up their worth can show before and after.

fields.label: My rules about appearance (if I looked..., then...)
Where each rule came from
Evidence from my own life for and against it
People I admire, and how much their looks have to do with it
How much of my self-worth appearance holds now (%)
What else I would like it to rest on

title: Body Gratitude Function List
summary: A list of what the client's body has carried them through, by life stage, written as a record rather than a rating.
goal: Build a history of the body as a companion rather than an object under review.
body_md: Move through life stages: childhood play, illness survived, work done, people carried, places reached. The tone is a record, not a pep talk. Clients with a history of harming or overworking their body may find this tender; slow down there. No comments on shape or size anywhere on the sheet.

fields.label: What my body did for me as a child
What it has carried me through
What it lets me do that I would miss
Someone it has held or helped
Something it recovered from
What I would like to thank it for, plainly

title: Media Diet Audit
summary: An inventory of the accounts, shows and images the client consumes, and what each does to how they feel in their body.
goal: Change what the client feeds their body image, since much of it arrives through a screen.
body_md: Go through the phone together. For each account or habit, ask what it does to the client's body feeling in the ten minutes after. Unfollowing is a real intervention and often the fastest one; replace, do not just remove, so the feed is not empty. Repeat in a month.

fields.label: Accounts and shows I see most
How I feel in my body after each (better, worse, nothing)
The ones that leave me comparing
Accounts I will unfollow or mute this week
What I will follow instead (bodies doing things, other interests entirely)
How my feed feels after the change

title: Life Roles Balance Wheel
summary: A wheel diagram where a client rates how balanced work, family, health and other life roles feel right now.
goal: Use it to open a conversation about which roles are running on empty and what to shift first.
body_md: The client rates satisfaction in six to eight roles — partner, parent, worker, friend, self-care and so on — on a scale from zero to ten, marks each on a spoke of the wheel, then connects the points. An uneven wheel becomes the starting point for talking about which roles are quietly being neglected and what the client is willing to change first. Bring it back in a later session to see what moved.

fields.label: List the roles you want to rate (work, parent, partner, friend, health, and so on)
Which role scored the lowest, and what does that tell you?
Which role scored the highest, and what is going right there?
What is one small change you could make in the lowest-scoring role this week?
What would need to be true for the wheel to look more balanced?

title: Motivation Readiness Ruler
summary: A 0-10 scale a client marks twice, once for how important a change feels and once for how confident they feel making it.
goal: Use it to locate exactly where ambivalence about a change is sitting so you can work there.
body_md: The client marks importance and confidence separately on two zero-to-ten lines, then explains why the number is not one point lower — that answer holds their own reasons for change, which land better coming from them than from you. A low confidence score with high importance points straight at where to focus the next few sessions.

fields.label: The change you are considering
How important does this change feel right now, 0 to 10?
Why is that number not one point lower?
How confident do you feel you could make this change, 0 to 10?
What would move that confidence number up by one point?

title: Cue-Anchored Routine Sheet
summary: Attaches a new habit to a routine the client already does automatically, rather than a fresh time slot.
goal: Use it to make a new habit easier to start by borrowing momentum from an existing one.
body_md: The client names a habit already running on autopilot — making coffee, brushing teeth, sitting down at a desk — and attaches the new behavior right after it: “after I pour my coffee, I will write down three tasks.” Anchoring to an existing cue removes the need to remember a new time, which is usually where habit plans fall apart. Review which anchors held and which need a different cue.

fields.label: The new habit you want to build
An existing routine that happens reliably, every day
Your plan: “After I ___, I will ___”
What might interrupt this plan, and what is the backup?
How did the anchor hold up this week?

title: Transition Readiness Checklist
summary: Walks a client through the practical and emotional pieces of an upcoming life change before it arrives.
goal: Use it to surface what a client has already prepared for a transition and what still needs attention.
body_md: Useful ahead of a move, a job change, a divorce finalizing, a retirement or any date the client has been counting down to. The checklist separates practical items (paperwork, logistics, people to notify) from emotional ones (what they are grieving, what they are relieved to leave, who they will lean on) so neither gets crowded out by the other. Revisit it as the date gets closer.

fields.label: What is changing, and when?
Practical steps still outstanding
What you expect to miss
What you expect to be relieved to leave behind
Who you can lean on in the first weeks after
One thing that would make the transition feel less abrupt

title: Weekly Self-Care Menu
summary: A client-built menu of restorative activities sorted by how much time and energy each one takes.
goal: Use it to give a client options that fit a five-minute gap as well as a free afternoon.
body_md: Self-care plans that only list big-ticket items — a spa day, a weekend away — rarely get used on an ordinary Tuesday. The client instead sorts activities into three columns by time cost: five minutes, thirty minutes, and a half day, so there is always something on the menu that fits the moment. Pin it somewhere visible and check in on which column gets used most.

fields.label: Five-minute options
Thirty-minute options
Half-day options
What usually stops you from using this list?
Which column did you actually use this week?

title: Should Statements Audit
summary: Lists the self-imposed ‘should’ rules a client is carrying and tests each one for whose voice it is in.
goal: Use it to loosen rigid self-imposed rules that are driving guilt or resentment.
body_md: ‘Should’ statements often turn out to be inherited rather than chosen — a parent’s standard, an old boss’s expectation, a cultural message never examined. The client lists their current shoulds, then for each one traces where it came from and rates how much it still serves them. A rule that scores low on ‘still serves me’ is a candidate for rewriting into a preference instead of a demand.

fields.label: A ‘should’ statement you catch yourself using often
Where do you think this rule came from?
What happens inside you when you break this rule?
How well does this rule actually serve you now, and why?
Rewrite it as a preference rather than a demand

title: Prediction Accuracy Tracker
summary: A running log comparing what a client predicted would happen against what actually happened.
goal: Use it to build evidence, one entry at a time, that anxious predictions overstate the odds.
body_md: Before a feared situation, the client writes down the specific prediction and how certain they feel of it. Afterward they log what actually happened and re-rate their certainty. Kept over a few weeks, the pattern usually does more to shift belief than any single conversation could, because the client is looking at their own track record rather than taking your word for it.

fields.label: The situation you are about to face
Your specific prediction
How certain are you, 0 to 100 percent?
What actually happened
Was your prediction right, partly right, or wrong?

title: Selective Attention Log
summary: Tracks moments a client noticed only the negative in a situation that also held neutral or positive evidence.
goal: Use it to show a client what their attention is filtering out, not just what it lets through.
body_md: After a hard moment, the client writes down what they noticed first, then goes back and lists what else was actually present — a compliment that got skipped past, a thing that went fine, a neutral fact read as bad news. The point is not that the negative did not happen, but that attention narrowed around it. Over several entries, a pattern of what the filter tends to catch usually shows up.

fields.label: The moment and what you noticed first
What else was actually present that you skipped past
Why do you think your attention went where it did?
What would you notice first if you were in a good mood?

title: Core Belief Timeline
summary: Maps when a long-held belief about the self first took shape and what has fed it since.
goal: Use it to trace a core belief back to its origin instead of treating it as simply true.
body_md: The client draws a line from childhood to now and marks moments that seem to have built the belief — an early message, a repeated comparison, a formative event — alongside moments that contradicted it and got waved away. Seeing the belief as something assembled over time, rather than a fact about them, is often the first crack in it. Pair with ongoing evidence-gathering work.

fields.label: The core belief you are examining
The earliest moment you can trace it to
Other moments along the way that reinforced it
Moments that contradicted it — what happened to those?
Whose voice does this belief sound like?

title: Graded Task Ladder
summary: Breaks one overwhelming task into small enough steps that the first one is almost too easy to skip.
goal: Use it to get a stalled task moving again by lowering the size of the first step, not the standard.
body_md: The client names the task that has been avoided, then works backward to a first step small enough to complete in under five minutes — opening the document, not writing the report. Each rung of the ladder should feel only slightly harder than the one before it. Momentum, not motivation, is the target: the ladder exists to be climbed on a day motivation is nowhere in sight.

fields.label: The task you have been avoiding
Step 1 — small enough to do in under five minutes
Step 2
Step 3
Step 4
What will you do right after finishing step 1, to keep going?

title: Tug-of-War With the Monster
summary: A classic ACT metaphor sheet: pulling harder against a painful feeling only pulls the client closer to it.
goal: Use it to introduce the idea that dropping the rope, not winning, is what loosens a struggle.
body_md: The client pictures a tug-of-war against a monster representing an unwanted feeling, with a pit between them. Pulling harder does not create distance — it only tightens the rope. The move that changes anything is dropping the rope altogether, which does not make the monster disappear but ends the exhausting pull. Use it to open a conversation about where a client keeps pulling instead of dropping the rope.

fields.label: What is the monster on the other end of your rope?
How hard have you been pulling, and for how long?
What has pulling harder actually gotten you?
What would dropping the rope look like this week?

title: Raisin Moment Practice
summary: A short sensory exercise, noticing one small object fully, used to teach present-moment attention.
goal: Use it to give a client a concrete, repeatable way to practice noticing rather than thinking about.
body_md: The client spends a few slow minutes with one small object — a raisin, a coin, a leaf — noticing texture, weight, smell and sound before doing anything else with it. The exercise is not about the object; it is a rehearsal for bringing that same quality of attention to a meal, a conversation or a walk later. Debrief what pulled attention away and how many times it was brought back.

fields.label: The object you practiced with
What did you notice that you would normally miss?
How many times did your mind wander, and to where?
Where else could you practice this kind of attention this week?

title: Values Versus Goals Sorter
summary: Sorts a client’s list of ‘things I want’ into values, which are directions, and goals, which are destinations.
goal: Use it to separate an ongoing direction from a one-time finish line so values survive an unmet goal.
body_md: A goal can be reached and closed — get the job, finish the degree. A value cannot, because it is a direction rather than a destination, like ‘being a supportive parent.’ The client sorts their list into the two columns and, for each goal, names the value underneath it. When a goal falls through, the value is still there to act on, which keeps a setback from feeling like the whole thing collapsed.

fields.label: List the things you have been striving for
Sort each into Goal (can be finished) or Value (ongoing direction)
For each goal, what value sits underneath it?
If this goal fell through tomorrow, how could you still act on the value?

title: Cost of Control Log
summary: Tracks what a client gives up each time they work hard to avoid or control an unwanted feeling.
goal: Use it to add up the real cost of control efforts that have not actually worked.
body_md: Every time a client cancels a plan, avoids a conversation or numbs out to keep a feeling away, something else gets spent — time, a relationship, a step toward something that mattered. The log tracks the control effort and its price side by side. Over several entries the total cost usually becomes more persuasive than any argument that the avoidance is not working.

fields.label: What you did to avoid or control the feeling
The feeling you were trying to avoid
What did it cost you — time, a relationship, an opportunity?
Did the feeling actually go away, or come back?

title: Values-Aligned Weekly Planner
summary: A weekly planner where each scheduled block gets tagged with the value it serves.
goal: Use it to make values visible in an ordinary week instead of living only as a list.
body_md: Alongside the usual weekly grid, each planned block gets a one-word tag naming the value it moves toward — connection, health, creativity, and so on. At the end of the week the client can see which values actually got time and which stayed on paper only. It is less a productivity tool than a mirror on where a week’s hours actually went.

fields.label: Your top three to five values right now
This week’s planned blocks and the value each one serves
Which value got the least time this week?
One block you could add next week for that value

title: Building Mastery Activity Log
summary: Logs one activity a day that builds a sense of competence, chosen slightly harder than what feels easy.
goal: Use it to build emotional resilience through a steady sense that hard things are possible.
body_md: Building mastery is the DBT emotion regulation skill of doing something that takes real effort and doing it well, on purpose, to build a reserve of confidence before it is needed. The client picks one activity a day slightly harder than their comfort level and logs it along with how it felt to complete. Pick activities that are genuinely achievable — mastery, not failure, is the point.

fields.label: Today’s mastery activity
Why is this slightly harder than easy for you?
How did it feel to complete it?
What will tomorrow’s activity be?

title: Pros and Cons Before Acting Card
summary: A DBT distress tolerance card weighing the pros and cons of tolerating a crisis versus acting on the urge.
goal: Use it to slow a client down long enough to weigh both paths before either one is taken.
body_md: In a crisis moment, weighing pros and cons on the spot rarely happens on its own. The card walks through four boxes filled out ahead of time and reread in the moment: the pros of tolerating the distress, the cons of tolerating it, the pros of acting on the urge, and the cons of acting on it. Reading all four before moving keeps the decision from being made on the first box alone.

fields.label: The urge or crisis this card is for
Pros of tolerating the distress without acting
Cons of tolerating the distress without acting
Pros and cons of acting on the urge instead

title: Objectives Priorities Worksheet
summary: Has a client rank getting their objective, keeping the relationship and keeping self-respect before a hard conversation.
goal: Use it to pick the right script before, not after, a conversation that could go several ways.
body_md: Before a request or a boundary conversation, priorities are rarely equal: sometimes getting the outcome matters most, sometimes preserving the relationship does, sometimes it is walking away with self-respect intact. Ranking the three ahead of time changes how the conversation gets approached — pushing hard for an outcome reads differently than protecting a relationship above all. Use before scripting the actual conversation.

fields.label: The conversation you are preparing for
Rank: getting the outcome, keeping the relationship, keeping self-respect
What does that ranking change about how you will approach it?
What would you be willing to give up to protect your top priority?

title: Willingness Versus Willfulness Sheet
summary: Sorts a client’s recent responses to a hard reality into willing (working with it) and willful (fighting it).
goal: Use it to show a client the difference between accepting a reality and giving up on changing it.
body_md: Willingness is doing what the moment calls for, even reluctantly; willfulness is refusing to do what works because it feels unfair that it has to be done at all. Neither is about liking the situation. The client sorts a few recent responses to a hard reality into these two columns and looks at which one tends to move things forward and which tends to keep them stuck.

fields.label: The hard reality you are responding to
A recent response that was willful (fighting it)
A recent response that was willing (working with it)
Which column tends to move things forward for you?

title: Riding the Wave Practice
summary: Tracks an intense emotion’s rise and fall to show a client that feelings peak and pass without action.
goal: Use it to build tolerance for a feeling by watching it move rather than acting to make it stop.
body_md: The client rates the intensity of a strong emotion every few minutes without doing anything to change it, plotting the numbers as the wave rises, peaks and comes back down. Most intense emotions pass within twenty to thirty minutes if nothing is done to prolong them. Seeing the actual shape of the wave on paper is often more convincing than being told the feeling will pass.

fields.label: The emotion you are riding out, and what triggered it
Intensity at the start, 0 to 10
Intensity every five minutes after that
What did you notice about how the wave moved?

title: Financial Values Conversation Guide
summary: Structured prompts for a couple to talk about what money means to each of them before talking numbers.
goal: Use it to surface each partner’s money history before a budget conversation turns into a fight.
body_md: Money fights are often values fights wearing a budget’s clothes — one partner equates saving with safety, the other equates spending with freedom, and neither realizes the other has a coherent logic. Each partner answers the prompts separately first, then reads answers aloud without interrupting. The goal of the first pass is understanding each other’s money story, not agreeing on a plan.

fields.label: Partner A: what did money mean in the home you grew up in?
Partner B: what did money mean in the home you grew up in?
Partner A: what does spending money on yourself feel like?
Partner B: what does spending money on yourself feel like?
One thing you learned about your partner’s money story

title: In-Law Boundaries Sheet
summary: Has each partner name where extended family involvement feels supportive and where it feels intrusive.
goal: Use it to get a couple presenting a united front to extended family instead of negotiating in front of them.
body_md: Conflict about in-laws usually hides an unresolved question about which family unit comes first now. Each partner separately marks where extended family involvement feels welcome and where it crosses a line, then the two compare lists and draft one shared boundary to bring to the family together — never one partner enforcing it against the other’s relative alone.

fields.label: Partner A: where does extended family involvement feel supportive?
Partner A: where does it feel intrusive?
Partner B: where does extended family involvement feel supportive?
Partner B: where does it feel intrusive?
One boundary you will hold together, as a team

title: Desire Discrepancy Conversation Guide
summary: A low-pressure structure for a couple with mismatched desire to talk about it without either partner feeling blamed.
goal: Use it to open a stuck conversation about differing desire without it turning into a scorecard.
body_md: Mismatched desire is one of the more avoided couples topics because it so easily turns into blame in either direction. The guide has each partner describe what desire feels tied to for them — connection, stress, body image, timing — before either one raises frequency at all, so the conversation starts with understanding instead of a number. Best run in session first before being sent home.

fields.label: Partner A: what does feeling desired usually depend on for you?
Partner B: what does feeling desired usually depend on for you?
What gets in the way most often for each of you?
One thing each partner could do that would help, without pressure

title: Blended Family Roles Sheet
summary: Has each adult in a blended family name what role they are actually playing versus what they assumed they would.
goal: Use it to make unspoken assumptions about a stepparent’s role explicit before they cause conflict.
body_md: Stepparent role confusion — disciplinarian, friend, bystander — is a common source of blended-family friction, often because nobody ever agreed on it out loud. Each adult writes the role they think they are playing and the role they think the children see them playing; differences between those columns are usually where the tension lives. Bring the children’s perspective in separately when appropriate.

fields.label: Adult 1: what role do you think you are playing day to day?
Adult 2: what role do you think you are playing day to day?
What role do you think the children actually see each of you in?
Where do those roles clash, and what would help?

title: Long-Distance Connection Planner
summary: Helps a couple living apart schedule the kinds of connection that a shared home usually provides by default.
goal: Use it to replace the incidental closeness of shared space with something deliberate.
body_md: Couples sharing a home get connection almost by accident — a hallway conversation, a shared meal. Distance removes that, and video calls alone rarely replace it. The planner has the couple name specific kinds of connection they are missing — parallel activity, physical affection, daily check-ins, a plan for the next visit — and schedule a concrete way to approximate each one.

fields.label: What kind of closeness do you miss most from being together?
One way you could approximate it this week, apart
How often will you check in, and how?
When is your next time together, and what will you protect for it?

title: Friendship Skills Practice Cards
summary: Role-play cards a parent and child act out together, practicing one small friendship skill at a time.
goal: Use it to rehearse a specific social skill in a low-stakes setting before the child needs it at school.
body_md: Each card names one small scenario — joining a game already in progress, handling being left out, taking a turn — and the parent role-plays it with the child, switching roles so the child gets to practice both sides. Keep each round short and end on one the child pulled off well. The parent notes which scenarios still feel hardest so those get more practice.

fields.label: Which scenario did you practice today?
What did you try saying or doing?
What felt easy about it?
What felt hard about it?
Parent: which scenario should you practice again next time?

title: Growth Mindset Garden Craft
summary: A child plants a paper garden where mistakes become seeds that grow into things learned.
goal: Use it to give a young perfectionist a hands-on way to see a mistake as the start of something, not an ending.
body_md: The child draws or cuts out a garden bed and, each time a mistake comes up in session or at home, adds a paper seed labeled with what the mistake was. Over following sessions, seeds that the child has learned something from get a flower drawn on top. The garden grows messier before it grows prettier, which is the point: mistakes are what the garden is made of, not weeds pulled out of it.

fields.label: What mistake will you plant as a seed today?
What did this mistake teach you?
Which seeds in your garden have grown into flowers?
Parent: which seed are you proud of your child for planting?

title: Family Feelings Check-In Chart
summary: A visual chart the whole family uses at dinner to name one feeling each, in a few words or a color.
goal: Use it to normalize naming feelings out loud as an ordinary family habit, not a special occasion.
body_md: Posted somewhere the family gathers, the chart gives everyone — parents included — a fast way to name a feeling with a word or a color rather than a full explanation. A rule of no follow-up questions unless the person offers more keeps it low-pressure enough that kids keep using it. Over time it becomes easier for a child to bring up a harder feeling because naming small ones is already routine.

fields.label: Today’s feeling, in one word or color: Family Member 1
Today’s feeling, in one word or color: Family Member 2
Today’s feeling, in one word or color: Family Member 3
Did anyone want to say more about theirs?

title: Team Family Motto Poster
summary: The family designs and decorates a shared motto that names how they want to treat each other.
goal: Use it to give a family a shared, visible reminder they helped write themselves.
body_md: Rather than a rule handed down, the family brainstorms together what they want to be known for — ‘we try again’, ‘we listen first’ — and votes on a short motto everyone had a hand in. Decorating and posting it somewhere visible matters as much as the words: a motto the kids helped design gets referenced far more often than a poster of house rules that arrived already finished.

fields.label: What words or phrases did each person suggest?
Which one did the family choose, and why?
How will you decorate the poster?
Where will it go, and who will remind the family to look at it?

title: Sibling Peace Treaty Worksheet
summary: Siblings draft a simple, decorated agreement about how they will handle disagreements between them.
goal: Use it to give siblings language for conflict that a parent did not write for them.
body_md: With a parent facilitating rather than dictating, siblings each name one thing that bothers them about fighting with the other and one thing they are willing to try differently. The ‘treaty’ gets written in the children’s own words and decorated like a real document, which gives it more weight than a verbal rule ever manages. Revisit and revise it as needed rather than treating it as final.

fields.label: Sibling 1: what bothers you most about our fights?
Sibling 2: what bothers you most about our fights?
Sibling 1: one thing I will try differently
Sibling 2: one thing I will try differently
How will we handle it if the treaty gets broken?

title: Strengths Bingo
summary: A bingo card of character strengths where a group fills a square each time they spot that strength in someone.
goal: Use it to get a group noticing and naming strengths in each other out loud.
body_md: Each square names a strength — patience, humor, honesty, creativity — and players mark it when they see a group member display it during the session or activity, then say so out loud before marking the square. It turns strength-spotting into something active rather than a static list, and the debrief usually surfaces strengths a member did not know others noticed in them.

fields.label: Which square did you fill first, and who earned it?
Which strength did you notice in yourself today?
Which strength surprised you to hear named about you?
What was it like to be the one naming strengths out loud?

title: Scenario Freeze Frame
summary: A group acts out a hard scenario, freezes on cue, and the group discusses the character’s options from there.
goal: Use it to practice recognizing choice points inside a conflict before it escalates further.
body_md: Two group members act out a scenario — a disagreement, a tempting shortcut, a tense conversation — and the facilitator calls ‘freeze’ at a turning point. The group discusses what the character could do next and why, then the scene resumes with a chosen option played out. Freezing mid-scene, rather than only debriefing after, keeps the choice point concrete instead of abstract.

fields.label: What scenario did you act out?
Where did the group call freeze, and what was happening?
What options did the group come up with?
Which option did you choose to play out, and how did it go?

title: The Support Web Game
summary: A group passes a ball of yarn while naming someone who supports them, building a visible web of connection.
goal: Use it to make a group’s web of support visible and concrete rather than an idea talked about.
body_md: Standing in a circle, each person holds the string, names a person or source of support in their life, and tosses the ball to someone else while keeping hold of their strand — building a literal web across the group. The debrief looks at how tangled and connected the web became, and what it felt like to be one strand holding the others up. A classic group-therapy opener for talking about support networks.

fields.label: Who or what did you name as support?
What did the web look like by the end?
What was it like to hold a strand that others depended on?
Who in your life outside this room could you add to your own web?

title: Coping Skills Jeopardy
summary: A quiz-style game where teams answer coping-skills questions across categories for points.
goal: Use it to review a group’s coping skills vocabulary in a competitive, low-pressure format.
body_md: Categories might include Grounding, Distress Tolerance, and Thinking Traps, with point values tied to difficulty. Teams buzz in to answer, and correct answers include a quick real example, not just the definition, so the game reinforces application rather than memorization. Works well as a mid-course review of skills covered so far.

fields.label: Which category did your team pick first, and why?
A question your team got right — what was the skill?
A question your team missed — what is the right answer?
Which skill do you want to practice more after playing?

title: Pass the Story Coping Chain
summary: A group builds one collaborative story, each person adding a line where the character uses a coping skill.
goal: Use it to practice naming coping strategies out loud inside a low-pressure, playful format.
body_md: One person starts a story with a character facing a stressful moment; each following person adds one line, and every third turn the added line has to include the character using a coping skill. The story usually gets funnier and stranger as it goes, which is part of the point — coping skills get rehearsed without the exercise feeling like a worksheet. Debrief which skills came up most.

fields.label: What was the story about?
Which coping skills showed up in the story?
Which one would you actually use yourself?
What made this easier or harder than just listing skills?

title: Orienting to Now Practice
summary: A grounding worksheet that has a client name concrete present-day details to signal to the body that the danger has passed.
goal: Use it to interrupt a flashback or a flooded moment by anchoring attention in the present.
body_md: The client lists concrete facts that could only be true right now — today’s date, the room they are in, three things they can see — to help the body register that the present is not the past. Run it first in session so the client has felt it work before trying it alone. If distress escalates toward a crisis, the client’s safety plan and 988 (call or text) are the next step, not this worksheet.

fields.label: Today’s date and where you are right now
Three things you can see around you
One thing that reminds you this is not then
How did your body feel before and after this practice?
If distress keeps rising, who or what do you turn to next?

title: Then Versus Now Thought Sort
summary: Sorts intrusive trauma-related thoughts into a ‘made sense then’ column and a ‘not true now’ column.
goal: Use it to separate a survival belief that was accurate then from its accuracy now.
body_md: Beliefs formed to survive a dangerous situation — ‘nobody is safe’, ‘I have to stay alert’ — made sense at the time and can outlast the danger. The client sorts current intrusive thoughts into what made sense then versus what is actually true now, without needing to describe the event itself. The sort itself, not the story behind it, is the therapeutic move.

fields.label: A thought that shows up often
Made sense then — why?
True now — yes or no, and why?
What is actually true about your safety today?

title: Making Room for the Alarm
summary: An acceptance practice for making room for the body’s alarm sensations without fighting or fixing them.
goal: Use it to reduce the added suffering that comes from fighting the body’s alarm response itself.
body_md: Trauma often leaves the body’s alarm system primed to fire even when nothing dangerous is happening. Fighting the alarm — trying to force it off — tends to make it louder. The client practices making room for the sensation, breathing around it rather than against it, while doing one small values-aligned action anyway. No detail of the original event is needed for this practice to work.

fields.label: Where do you notice the alarm in your body?
What is your usual move against it — fight, flee, numb?
Practice making room for it for one minute — what did you notice?
What is one small action you could still take with the alarm present?

title: Paired Muscle Relaxation for Hyperarousal
summary: A brief muscle tension-and-release sequence used to bring down physical hyperarousal after a trauma trigger.
goal: Use it to give the body a fast, physical off-ramp when hyperarousal has already taken over.
body_md: When a trigger has already activated the body — racing heart, tight chest, restlessness — talking is often the wrong first move. The client tenses one muscle group hard for five seconds, then releases, moving through the body head to feet, pairing each release with a slow exhale. The physical shift usually needs to happen before any cognitive work can land. Practice it calm first, before it is needed in a spike.

fields.label: Where in your body do you feel the activation first?
Rate the intensity before starting, 0 to 10
Which muscle groups did you tense and release?
Rate the intensity after, 0 to 10

title: Trauma-Informed Partner Support Plan
summary: A plan a couple builds together for what actually helps when one partner is triggered, made in a calm moment.
goal: Use it to give a supporting partner a concrete plan instead of guessing what helps in the moment.
body_md: Built when both partners are calm, this plan names what the triggered partner finds helpful — space, a specific phrase, physical touch or its absence — and what to avoid, such as pressing for details or minimizing. The supporting partner is not asked to understand the trauma itself, only to follow the plan the way it is written. Revisit and adjust the plan as the couple learns more about what helps.

fields.label: Partner A: what helps you most when you are triggered?
Partner A: what makes it worse?
Partner B: what do you need to hear or do to feel useful in that moment?
A phrase either of you can use to signal ‘I need the plan right now’

title: Anxiety Fuel Log
summary: Tracks daily habits, sleep, caffeine, avoidance and reassurance-seeking, that tend to raise or lower anxiety.
goal: Use it to find the everyday inputs a client can adjust rather than only the anxious thoughts.
body_md: Anxiety is shaped by more than thoughts — sleep debt, caffeine, skipped meals and avoidance all raise the baseline. The client logs a few of these inputs alongside a daily anxiety rating for a week or two, then looks for the inputs that track most closely with the highs and lows. Small changes to inputs are often easier for a client to start with than changing the anxious thoughts directly.

fields.label: Hours of sleep last night
Caffeine today
Any avoidance today, and of what?
Overall anxiety today, 0 to 10
What pattern are you starting to notice?

title: What If Ladder
summary: Arranges a client’s catastrophic ‘what if’ thoughts from mild to most feared and tests each in turn.
goal: Use it to work through a chain of anxious predictions instead of getting stuck on the worst one.
body_md: Anxious thinking often runs a chain — ‘what if I’m late’ leads to ‘what if I get fired’ leads to ‘what if I lose everything’ — and the client’s attention snags on the worst link. Laying the chain out as a ladder lets each link get examined for how likely it actually is, one rung at a time, rather than reacting to the whole chain at once.

fields.label: Your starting worry
What if that happens — then what?
What if that happens — then what?
How likely is the worst rung, realistically?
What would you actually do if the worst rung happened?

title: Worry Weather Forecast
summary: Reframes anxious thoughts as changeable weather passing through, rather than a forecast of what will happen.
goal: Use it to build distance from anxious thoughts by treating them as weather, not fact.
body_md: The client names today’s ‘mental weather’ — stormy, foggy, clear with a few clouds — as a way of holding anxious thoughts lightly rather than as literal predictions. Weather always passes, which is the point: today’s storm is not tomorrow’s forecast. Use it as a quick daily check-in that builds defusion without needing a long exercise each time.

fields.label: Today’s mental weather report
What thoughts came with that weather?
What would you do today even with this weather present?
How did the weather change by the end of the day?

title: Anxiety Opposite Action Card
summary: Applies the DBT opposite action skill to anxiety by naming the urge to avoid and the opposite move.
goal: Use it to interrupt avoidance before it has a chance to reinforce the anxiety further.
body_md: When the urge from anxiety does not fit the actual level of danger — a normal meeting, not a real threat — DBT’s opposite action skill has the client identify the avoidance urge and do the opposite, fully, with matching body language. Half-hearted opposite action tends not to work; the client practices approaching all the way in, not just partway.

fields.label: The situation and the anxious urge to avoid
Does the urge actually fit the danger here?
The opposite action, described fully
How did it go when you did the opposite action all the way?

title: Worry Backpack Unpacking Craft
summary: A child draws a backpack full of worries, then ‘unpacks’ one at a time to decide which ones to carry today.
goal: Use it to help a child sort worries into ones to carry and ones to set down for now.
body_md: The child draws or writes each worry as an item inside a backpack, then takes them out one at a time and sorts them into ‘carry today’ and ‘set down for now’ piles with the parent’s help. Not every worry needs solving in one sitting; the craft gives a child physical practice choosing which one gets attention right now. Keep the ‘set down’ worries somewhere to revisit later, not just dismissed.

fields.label: Draw your worry backpack — what worries are inside?
Pick one worry to unpack first — what is it?
Carry today or set down for now?
Parent: which worry will you check back in on tomorrow?

title: Low-Energy Day Menu
summary: A pre-planned list of very low-effort activities a client can turn to on the hardest, lowest-energy days.
goal: Use it to have a plan ready before a low day arrives, when planning feels hardest.
body_md: Depression tends to be worst exactly when the energy to make a plan is lowest, so the menu gets built on a better day for use on a worse one. Every item should take five minutes or less and require almost no decision-making — open the curtains, drink a glass of water, text one person a single emoji. The goal on a hard day is doing one item, not several.

fields.label: Five very low-effort items for your menu
Where will you keep this list so you can find it on a bad day?
On a hard day, which item did you manage?
How did doing even that one thing change the day?

title: Effort Versus Mood Log
summary: Tests the belief ‘I’ll do it once I feel like it’ by comparing outcomes when action came before mood.
goal: Use it to challenge the assumption that motivation has to arrive before action can start.
body_md: Depression often convinces a client that mood has to improve before action is possible, but the reverse is usually more reliable: action first, mood follows. The client logs a few activities attempted, noting whether they waited to feel like it first or acted anyway, and rates mood before and after either way. Most people find the ‘acted anyway’ entries score better than they expected.

fields.label: The activity
Did you wait to feel like it, or act first?
Mood before, 0 to 10
Mood after, 0 to 10
What does this entry tell you about waiting for motivation?

title: Values in the Fog Practice
summary: Helps a client name one values-aligned action to take even while depression makes everything feel flat.
goal: Use it to keep values-based action moving even when a client cannot access much feeling at all.
body_md: Depression can flatten access to feeling, including the satisfaction that usually rewards action, which is why waiting to ‘want to’ rarely works. The client names a value that still matters even in the fog and picks one small action in that direction, doing it without expecting to feel much yet. The action counts whether or not it produces a feeling — feeling can catch up later.

fields.label: A value that still matters, even now
One small action in that direction you could take today
Did you take the action? What happened?
Did you expect to feel something — did you?

title: Emotional Numbing Check-In
summary: A brief check-in for noticing emotional numbness and using one small sensory cue to reconnect.
goal: Use it to interrupt numbness with a small, deliberate sensory anchor rather than forcing a feeling.
body_md: Depression sometimes shows up less as sadness than as numbness — nothing registers much at all. Rather than trying to force a feeling, the client uses one deliberate sensory input — cold water on the wrists, a strong scent, bright light — and simply notices whatever small response shows up, without judging it as too small to count. Track what tends to work over several tries.

fields.label: What did numbness feel like today?
Which sensory cue did you try?
What, if anything, did you notice afterward?
Which cues seem to work best for you so far?

title: Pleasant Memory Trivia
summary: A group game where members take turns sharing and guessing details of each other’s pleasant memories.
goal: Use it to get a group actively recalling and sharing positive memories rather than only naming problems.
body_md: Each member shares a brief pleasant memory without saying when or where it happened; the group asks yes-or-no questions to guess details, turning recall into an active game rather than a static list. Depression narrows access to positive memory, so practicing retrieval, even playfully, is the point, not just hearing the memory once. Debrief which memories were hardest to think of.

fields.label: The pleasant memory you shared (briefly, for yourself)
What questions did the group ask to guess details?
How hard was it to think of a pleasant memory today?
What did you notice hearing others’ memories?

title: Time Blindness Check Card
summary: Compares a client’s time estimate for a task against the clock, building awareness of time blindness.
goal: Use it to make the gap between estimated and actual time visible instead of assumed.
body_md: Many people with ADHD consistently misjudge how long tasks take, in either direction, without realizing it, a pattern often called time blindness. The client estimates a task’s length before starting, times it, and logs both. Seeing the actual gap over several entries is usually more convincing than being told to ‘plan better,’ and it gives concrete numbers to pad future estimates with.

fields.label: The task
Your time estimate before starting
Actual time it took
How far off was your estimate?

title: Interest-Based Values Bridge
summary: Bridges a boring but necessary task to a value that actually matters, to help follow-through stick.
goal: Use it when interest alone will not carry a task, by connecting it to something the client values.
body_md: Motivation for many people with ADHD tracks interest more than importance, so a necessary-but-boring task can stall no matter how much it matters on paper. The client names the task, then traces a line to a value it actually serves — even a dull filing task can connect to ‘being someone people can rely on.’ The bridge will not make the task interesting, but it gives a reason worth returning to when attention drifts.

fields.label: The boring task you keep avoiding
What value does finishing this actually serve?
How does it feel to name that connection?
What is the smallest next step toward it?

title: Fidget Toolkit Planner
summary: A child tests a few fidget or movement tools and tracks which ones actually help them focus.
goal: Use it to find which sensory tools genuinely help a child’s focus rather than guessing.
body_md: Not every fidget tool helps every child, and some become a distraction rather than a support. Over a week, the child tries a different tool each day — a squeeze ball, a standing option, a chewable, a doodle pad — during a homework or focus task, and rates with the parent how well it worked. The goal is a short list of two or three tools worth keeping on hand, not a full collection.

fields.label: Today’s tool
What task were you using it during?
Did it help you focus? How much?
Parent: keep this tool on the list — yes or no?

title: Attention Scavenger Hunt
summary: A timed scavenger hunt game that rewards sustained visual attention rather than speed alone.
goal: Use it to practice sustained attention in a format that feels like play, not a demand.
body_md: Players search a room or a picture for a list of hidden items within a time limit, then compare finds and talk about what helped them keep scanning versus what pulled their attention away. Because the challenge is built into the game rather than assigned as a task, sustained attention gets practiced without the usual resistance that comes with ‘focus on this.’ Debrief what strategies helped.

fields.label: What items were you hunting for?
What helped you keep searching when it got hard?
What pulled your attention away?
What would help you focus even longer next time?

title: Executive Function Support Agreement
summary: A couple negotiates concrete ways one partner can support executive function without becoming a parent figure.
goal: Use it to turn ‘just be more organized’ into specific, agreed support both partners are comfortable with.
body_md: When one partner has ADHD, the other can drift into a caretaking or nagging role without either partner choosing it on purpose, which usually breeds resentment on both sides. The worksheet has each partner name specific supports that would actually help — a shared calendar, a standing reminder, first-refusal on reminders rather than repeated ones — and what would feel like being parented instead of supported.

fields.label: ADHD partner: what kind of support actually helps you?
ADHD partner: what crosses into feeling like being parented?
Other partner: what would make offering support feel less exhausting?
One specific support you will both try this week

title: High-Risk Situation Map
summary: Maps the places, people and times that tend to raise the risk of substance use, before they arrive.
goal: Use it to plan around high-risk situations instead of relying on willpower in the moment.
body_md: Urges rarely arrive at random — certain places, people, times of day or emotional states raise the odds substantially. The client maps their own pattern across these categories and, for each high-risk item, names one concrete plan: avoid it, bring support, or have an exit ready. The map becomes something to check before a risky weekend or event, not just an after-the-fact reflection.

fields.label: Places that raise your risk
People that raise your risk
Times or situations that raise your risk
For your top risk, what is your plan?

title: Urge Curve Prediction Sheet
summary: Has a client predict, then track, how long an urge actually lasts to challenge the sense that it never will.
goal: Use it to build evidence that urges peak and fall within a predictable window.
body_md: In the grip of an urge, it can feel permanent, which makes giving in seem like the only way out. Before it fades, the client predicts how long the urge will last; afterward they log the actual time. Most urges peak and fall within twenty to forty-five minutes if nothing is done to feed them. A few logged entries usually do more to shift the belief than being told urges pass.

fields.label: What triggered the urge?
Predicted length of the urge
Actual length before it faded
What did you do while riding it out?

title: Values Over Urges Card
summary: A pocket card linking one specific value to the moment an urge to use substances shows up.
goal: Use it to give a client a values-based reason to reach for in the exact moment an urge appears.
body_md: In the moment an urge appears, abstract commitments are hard to access, so the card keeps it concrete: one value, one reason it matters, written in the client’s own words, small enough to carry. The point is not to argue the urge away but to have something values-based ready to read in the ten seconds before a decision gets made either way.

fields.label: The value you want on this card
Why does this value matter to you, in your own words?
Where will you keep this card?
Did you read it during an urge this week? What happened?

title: Urge Distress Tolerance Menu
summary: A menu of quick distress tolerance skills a client picks from specifically when an urge to use is strong.
goal: Use it to have several fast options ready instead of one plan that might not fit the moment.
body_md: Not every distress tolerance skill fits every urge moment — sometimes intense sensation helps (TIPP), sometimes distraction does, sometimes it is simply calling someone. The client builds a short menu of their own best options ahead of time and picks whichever fits the moment an urge hits, rather than trying to remember a whole skill set under pressure.

fields.label: Your top three to five go-to skills for an urge moment
Which one did you use this week?
Did it help — how much, 0 to 10?
Any skill to add or drop from the menu?

title: Supporting Without Enabling Worksheet
summary: Helps a partner tell the difference between supportive help and behavior that enables continued substance use.
goal: Use it to give a supporting partner concrete lines between helping and enabling.
body_md: Partners of someone working on substance use often want to help and are unsure where support turns into covering for, lending money toward, or minimizing continued use. Each partner separately lists actions that feel supportive and actions that feel like enabling, then the two compare lists together, ideally with the clinician present for the first pass rather than doing it alone at home.

fields.label: Using partner: what kind of support actually helps you?
Supporting partner: what have you done that might be enabling?
What is one boundary the supporting partner needs to hold?
What support can continue without crossing into enabling?

title: Anger Repair Timeline
summary: Tracks how long it actually takes to repair after an outburst, and what shortens or lengthens that time.
goal: Use it to make the repair process itself, not just the outburst, something a client can improve.
body_md: An outburst is often treated as the whole event, but what happens in the hours and days after, an apology, a return to normal, rebuilt trust, matters just as much and is more within a client’s control. The client logs how long repair took after a recent episode and what specific action seemed to shorten it, building a record of what actually helps repair move faster next time.

fields.label: The episode
What did you do to start repair, and when?
How long did it take before things felt normal again?
What seemed to speed up or slow down the repair?

title: Fairness Assumption Check
summary: Tests the ‘this is unfair’ thought that often sits underneath anger, against the actual facts available.
goal: Use it to slow down the jump from perceived unfairness straight to an angry reaction.
body_md: Anger often runs on an assumption of unfairness or a broken rule that felt certain in the moment but was never checked. The client writes the fairness assumption behind a recent angry moment, then lists what evidence actually supports it and what other explanation could also fit. This is not about deciding the client was wrong to be angry, only about slowing the jump from assumption to reaction.

fields.label: The moment and the anger it triggered
What rule or fairness assumption felt broken?
What evidence actually supports that?
What is another explanation that could also fit?

title: Anger Wise Mind Pause Card
summary: A pause card that walks a client from emotion mind toward wise mind in the middle of an anger spike.
goal: Use it to interrupt the jump from trigger straight to reaction with one deliberate pause.
body_md: In an anger spike, emotion mind can take over fast, driving a reaction before wise mind gets a say. The card walks through a short sequence: notice the spike, name it as emotion mind, take one slow breath, and ask what wise mind would add to what emotion mind is saying. It will not stop the anger, but it buys the seconds needed for a choice instead of a reflex.

fields.label: What triggered the spike?
What was emotion mind saying?
After the pause, what did wise mind add?
What did you do instead of the first reaction?

title: Anger Thermometer Countdown
