summary: A thermometer chart where a child marks rising anger levels and picks a matching cool-down move at each one.
goal: Use it to give a child a specific action tied to each level of anger, not just one plan for all of it.
body_md: Rather than one cool-down strategy for all of anger, the thermometer has a different move at each level — deep breaths at a low simmer, a break in another room at a rolling boil, telling a grown-up before it reaches the top. The child and parent build the chart together on a calm day, then practice recognizing which level they are at before choosing the matching move.

fields.label: What does level 1 (a little annoyed) feel like in your body?
What move do you use at level 1?
What does level 3 (really mad) feel like?
What move do you use at level 3?
Parent: which level did you notice today, and did the move help?

title: Cool-Down Countdown Relay
summary: A relay game where each turn a player demonstrates a cool-down skill before passing to the next player.
goal: Use it to rehearse quick cool-down skills as a group, in a format that stays playful, not preachy.
body_md: Players take turns drawing a card naming a mild frustration and, before passing the turn along, demonstrating one cool-down skill on the spot — counting breaths, a shoulder shrug release, a short walk to a marker and back. Keeping it fast-paced and a little silly lowers the resistance kids and teens often have to anger skills practiced outside of an actual angry moment.

fields.label: Which frustration card did you draw?
Which cool-down skill did you demonstrate?
Which skill from the game felt most natural to you?
Which one would you actually reach for when really angry?

title: Certainty Seeking Cost Log
summary: Logs how much time checking, researching or mentally reviewing actually costs in a day.
goal: Use it to make the time cost of certainty-seeking visible instead of hidden inside a normal day.
body_md: Checking, researching and mental reviewing can eat far more of a day than a client realizes because each instance feels small on its own. The log tracks time spent on these certainty-seeking behaviors across a day or two, then totals it up. Seeing the number in minutes or hours often does more to motivate change than a general sense that ‘it’s a lot.’

fields.label: The certainty-seeking behavior
How long did it take?
Did it actually bring more certainty, or just relief that faded?
Total time today spent this way

title: Thought-Action Fusion Check
summary: Tests the belief that having a thought is as significant as acting on it, a common thread in intrusive thoughts.
goal: Use it to separate the fact of having a thought from any claim about what it means.
body_md: A thought crossing the mind and a thought reflecting intent or character are not the same thing, but intrusive thoughts can feel otherwise in the moment. The client writes the thought, then separately answers whether having it means they want it, and whether having it makes them a worse person. Most clients land on ‘having a thought is not the same as choosing it’ once it is laid out this plainly.

fields.label: The intrusive thought
Does having this thought mean you want it to happen? Why or why not?
Does having it say something bad about your character? Why or why not?
What would you tell a friend who had this same thought?

title: Sticky Thought Defusion Drill
summary: A defusion drill for ‘sticky’ intrusive thoughts that keep returning no matter how often they are dismissed.
goal: Use it to change a client’s relationship to a sticky thought rather than trying to make it stop.
body_md: Trying to push a sticky thought away tends to make it stick harder. The client instead practices noticing the thought and labeling it out loud — ‘I’m having the sticky thought that...’ — without arguing with it or trying to resolve it. The drill does not aim to make the thought go away; it aims to make having it feel less urgent and less like an emergency each time.

fields.label: The sticky thought
Say it with the label: ‘I’m having the sticky thought that...’
What is your urge right after — to check, to argue, to avoid?
What did you do instead of following the urge?

title: Uncertainty Tolerance Practice Log
summary: Logs small, deliberate practice sitting with uncertainty instead of resolving it through checking or reassurance.
goal: Use it to build tolerance for not knowing, one small deliberate exposure at a time.
body_md: OCD tends to promise that one more check or one more reassurance will finally bring certainty, which keeps the cycle going. The client picks one small, low-stakes moment of uncertainty to leave unresolved on purpose — an unchecked lock, an unanswered what-if — and logs how the discomfort moved without the usual resolving behavior. Start small; the skill is tolerance, not bravado.

fields.label: The uncertainty you left unresolved on purpose
Urge to check or seek reassurance, 0 to 10, at the start
How did the urge change over time without acting on it?
What did you learn from sitting with it?

title: Sticky Thought Jar Craft
summary: A child writes down sticky, repeating thoughts and puts them in a jar labeled ‘thoughts, not facts’.
goal: Use it to give a child a physical way to set aside a sticky thought without needing to act on it.
body_md: The child decorates a small jar and labels it ‘thoughts, not facts.’ When a sticky, repeating thought shows up, they write or draw it on a slip of paper and post it in the jar instead of checking, asking, or doing the thing the thought demands. The parent helps track how many slips go in the jar and celebrates moments a thought went in the jar instead of being acted on.

fields.label: What sticky thought showed up today?
Did it go in the jar instead of being acted on?
How did it feel to let the thought sit in the jar?
Parent: how many slips went in the jar this week?

title: Panic Symptom Reality Check Sheet
summary: Lists panic sensations next to what is actually happening in the body, to counter fear of imminent danger.
goal: Use it to replace a catastrophic reading of panic symptoms with an accurate physiological one.
body_md: A racing heart during panic can feel like a heart attack, and tight breathing can feel like suffocation, even though both are the body’s alarm system doing exactly what it is built to do. The sheet lists common panic sensations next to a plain explanation of what is actually happening physiologically. Reviewing it outside of an attack, when the fear is not active, helps it stick for use during one.

fields.label: A panic sensation you experience
What does it feel like is happening?
What is actually happening in the body?
How does knowing that change the sensation’s intensity?

title: Panic Attack Duration Tracker
summary: Tracks how long a panic attack actually lasts against how long it felt like it would last.
goal: Use it to build evidence that panic attacks peak and pass within a predictable window.
body_md: In the middle of an attack, it can feel endless, which fuels the fear that drives it higher. The client notes the start time, the estimated feared duration, and the actual time it took to come back down. Most panic attacks peak within ten minutes and pass within twenty to thirty. A logged history of actual durations is often more convincing than being told this in the moment.

fields.label: Start time
How long did it feel like it would last?
Actual time until it came back down
What helped it pass?

title: Willing Passenger Panic Practice
summary: Practices letting panic sensations be present in the background while still doing a values-based activity.
goal: Use it to keep panic sensations from automatically canceling a client’s plans.
body_md: The instinct during panic is to stop everything until the sensations pass, which can end up shrinking a client’s life around avoiding the next attack. The practice has the client name one activity that matters and do it with the panic sensations present, treating them as an unwelcome passenger rather than the driver. The sensations are not fought or denied, just not obeyed as an order to stop.

fields.label: The activity that matters to you
What sensations showed up while doing it?
Did you keep going anyway? What happened?
What did this practice teach you about the sensations’ actual power?

title: Paced Exhale Panic Card
summary: A breathing card with a longer exhale than inhale, used right at the first sign of a panic attack.
goal: Use it to slow the body’s alarm response at the earliest moment an attack is building.
body_md: A longer exhale than inhale signals the body’s calming system to engage, which can blunt a panic attack before it fully builds. The client practices a count of in for four, out for six, several times a day when calm so the pattern is already familiar, then reaches for it at the very first sign of an attack rather than waiting until it has taken over.

fields.label: Practiced today, calm — how many rounds?
Did you notice early signs of an attack this week?
Did you use the breathing pattern? What happened?
How does the pattern feel different practiced calm versus in a spike?

title: First Response Card for Partners
summary: A short, agreed script a partner uses in the first moments of noticing a panic attack starting.
goal: Use it so a supporting partner has an agreed first move instead of improvising under pressure.
body_md: The first response to a partner’s panic attack matters — some reactions help, others unintentionally add pressure (‘calm down,’ repeated questions). Built together outside of an attack, the card names the exact first move the supporting partner should make and a short phrase to say, agreed on in advance so neither partner is guessing in the moment.

fields.label: Partner having attacks: what is genuinely helpful right at the start?
Partner having attacks: what makes it worse?
Supporting partner: what will your first move be?
The agreed phrase you will say

title: Parent Battery Check
summary: Has a parent rate their own capacity before reacting, since the same behavior lands differently depending on it.
goal: Use it to help a parent notice their own state before choosing a response, not just the child’s behavior.
body_md: The same misbehavior can get a very different response depending on how depleted the parent already is, which children usually cannot see and parents often do not track. Before responding to a flashpoint, the parent rates their own battery level and considers whether the plan they are about to use matches a low-battery day or assumes a full one. Sometimes the answer is simply to pause before responding at all.

fields.label: Your battery level right now, 0 to 10
What is happening with your child?
What response were you about to use?
Does that response fit your current battery level?

title: Child Behavior Reframe Sheet
summary: Tests a parent’s interpretation of a child’s behavior against other explanations that could also fit.
goal: Use it to loosen an interpretation of a child’s behavior that is fueling a parent’s own anger.
body_md: ‘He’s doing this on purpose’ and ‘she can’t handle this right now’ point to very different parental responses, even for the same behavior. The parent writes down their current read of a repeated frustrating behavior, then lists at least one other explanation that fits the facts equally well — a skill gap, an unmet need, a developmental stage. The goal is a wider set of options, not necessarily a kinder one.

fields.label: The behavior
Your current interpretation of why they do it
One other explanation that fits equally well
Which interpretation would you rather respond from?

title: Parenting Values Compass Check
summary: Compares the parent a client wants to be with how they actually showed up in a recent hard moment.
goal: Use it to close the gap between parenting values and a moment-to-moment reaction without shame.
body_md: In a hard parenting moment, values are easy to lose track of under stress. The client names the kind of parent they want to be — patient, present, firm and warm — then looks honestly at a recent hard moment and how close it landed to that. The point is not guilt over the gap but using it to choose what to try differently next time, values still intact.

fields.label: The kind of parent you want to be, in a few words
A recent hard moment — what actually happened?
How close did that land to the parent you want to be?
What would help you close that gap next time?

title: Parenting Team Huddle Sheet
summary: A short, regular check-in where co-parents align on approach before the next flashpoint, not during it.
goal: Use it to get co-parents on the same page ahead of time instead of negotiating in front of the child.
body_md: Disagreeing about parenting in front of a child undermines both parents and confuses the child about which rule holds. The huddle is a short, regular check-in, five minutes, not a summit, where co-parents name one upcoming flashpoint and agree on the approach in advance, so a united response is ready before the moment arrives rather than improvised during it.

fields.label: An upcoming flashpoint you expect this week
Parent A’s usual approach to it
Parent B’s usual approach to it
The approach you are agreeing to use together

title: Grown-Up and Me Feelings Match
summary: A matching game where parent and child each guess what feeling fits a shared family moment from the week.
goal: Use it to build a shared feelings vocabulary between parent and child through play, not lecture.
body_md: Parent and child each write down a few moments from the week on separate cards, then take turns guessing what feeling the other person had in that moment before comparing notes. Parents are often surprised by what a child actually felt, and children enjoy getting to ‘guess’ a grown-up’s feelings for once. Keep it playful; being wrong is part of the game, not a failure.

fields.label: A moment from this week (child)
What feeling do you think the grown-up had? (child guesses)
A moment from this week (parent)
What feeling do you think the child had? (parent guesses)
What did you learn about each other’s feelings?

title: New Parent Reality Versus Expectation Sheet
summary: Compares what a new parent expected postpartum life to feel like against what it has actually been.
goal: Use it to name the gap between expectation and reality without treating the gap as a personal failure.
body_md: New-parent expectations are often shaped by curated images and other people’s highlight reels, and the gap between that and an actual postpartum reality can quietly feed shame. The client writes what they expected next to what has actually happened, in a few key areas — sleep, bonding, identity, support — and names the gap plainly rather than treating it as evidence something is wrong with them.

fields.label: What did you expect this stage to feel like?
What has it actually felt like?
Where is the biggest gap?
What would help close that gap, even a little?

title: Postpartum Guilt Thought Log
summary: A thought log built around the specific guilt thoughts that show up often in the postpartum period.
goal: Use it to examine postpartum guilt thoughts with the same rigor as any other automatic thought.
body_md: ‘I should be enjoying this more’ and ‘a good parent wouldn’t feel this way’ are common postpartum automatic thoughts that rarely get the same scrutiny other anxious or depressive thoughts get, because they can feel like facts about being a bad parent. The client logs the thought, the evidence for and against it, and a more balanced alternative, the same way any other thought record works.

fields.label: The guilt thought
Evidence that supports it
Evidence against it
A more balanced thought

title: Good Enough Parent Practice
summary: Practices holding a perfectionistic new-parent standard more lightly, in favor of a workable ‘good enough’.
goal: Use it to loosen an all-or-nothing new-parent standard that is driving exhaustion or guilt.
body_md: New parents often carry an unspoken standard of doing everything right, which nothing in an actual postpartum period can meet. The client names the standard, then practices noticing it as a thought — ‘I’m having the thought that a good parent would...’ — rather than a rule, and identifies what ‘good enough’ would actually look like today instead of the unreachable ideal.

fields.label: The standard you are holding yourself to
Say it as a thought: ‘I’m having the thought that...’
What would ‘good enough’ look like today instead?
What gets easier if ‘good enough’ is actually enough?

title: Postpartum PLEASE Check
summary: Adapts the DBT PLEASE skill to newborn care, where sleep and eating rarely follow a normal schedule.
goal: Use it to track basic physical needs realistically, given what newborn care actually allows.
body_md: PLEASE, treating physical illness, eating, avoiding mood-altering substances, sleep and exercise, assumes a baseline that newborn care regularly disrupts, especially sleep. Rather than aiming for an ideal, the client tracks what was realistically possible each day and names one small thing that is actually within reach, given a newborn’s schedule, not an adult’s.

fields.label: Sleep today — how much, in whatever pieces it came in
Did you eat something today? What?
Any physical symptoms you are ignoring?
One realistic thing you could add tomorrow, given the baby’s schedule

title: Postpartum Labor Rebalance Sheet
summary: A concrete worksheet for rebalancing night wakings and household tasks after a birth, not just talking about it.
goal: Use it to turn a vague ‘we should split things more evenly’ into a specific, written plan.
body_md: Vague agreements to ‘share more’ tend to dissolve under exhaustion, while a specific written plan holds up better. The couple lists the recurring tasks of the newborn period — night wakings, feeding, household chores, outside support coordination — and assigns or alternates each one concretely, revisiting the plan every couple of weeks as things change fast in this period.

fields.label: List the recurring tasks of this period
Who currently does most of each, and how does that feel?
How will you split or alternate each task going forward?
When will you revisit this plan?

title: Self-Worth Sources Inventory
summary: Inventories where a client’s current sense of worth comes from, and where they would rather it come from.
goal: Use it to make an unexamined source of self-worth, often achievement or approval, visible and open to change.
body_md: Self-worth quietly tied to performance, appearance or others’ approval tends to feel shaky, because all three can be taken away or withheld. The client lists what their worth currently seems to depend on, then names what they would rather it be grounded in instead — effort, values, character. The gap between the two lists becomes a direction to work toward, not a verdict on the client.

fields.label: What does your sense of worth currently seem to depend on?
What happens to your worth when that thing dips or disappears?
What would you rather your worth be grounded in?
One way to practice grounding worth there this week

title: Compliment Deflection Log
summary: Tracks moments a client deflected or dismissed a compliment, and practices simply accepting it instead.
goal: Use it to interrupt the automatic habit of arguing with positive feedback.
body_md: Deflecting a compliment — ‘oh, it was nothing,’ ‘anyone could have done it’ — can become so automatic that a client stops registering positive feedback at all. The log tracks compliments received, the automatic deflection, and a practiced alternative response of simply saying thank you without qualifying it. Even a client who does not believe the compliment yet can practice the behavior of accepting it.

fields.label: The compliment you received
What did you automatically say or think?
What would ‘just saying thank you’ have sounded like?
Did you practice accepting it this week? What happened?

title: Self-As-Context Strengths Practice
summary: Uses the observing-self perspective to notice a harsh self-verdict without becoming fused with it.
goal: Use it to give a client distance from a self-critical verdict by practicing the observer’s view.
body_md: The part of a person that notices a thought is not the same as the thought itself — the observing self watching ‘I’m worthless’ is not, itself, worthless. The client practices stepping back to that observer position when a harsh self-verdict shows up, noticing the verdict rather than being it. This is a stance to practice repeatedly, not a one-time insight that resolves the verdict.

fields.label: The self-verdict that showed up
From the observer’s seat, what do you notice about having this thought?
Is the observer the same thing as the verdict, or something that notices it?
What changed, stepping back to notice rather than agreeing?

title: Kindness Toward Myself Mirror Craft
summary: A child decorates a mirror frame with kind phrases to read to themselves, practiced daily with a parent.
goal: Use it to build a habit of self-kindness through repetition, before a child can explain why it matters.
body_md: The child chooses a few kind phrases — ‘I am learning,’ ‘mistakes are okay,’ ‘I am proud of me’ — and decorates a small mirror frame or card with them, placing it somewhere they will see it daily, like a bathroom mirror. The parent practices saying the phrases along with the child at first, since children often need to hear kindness modeled before they can offer it to themselves.

fields.label: What kind phrases did you pick?
Where will you keep your mirror or card?
Did you say your phrases today? How did it feel?
Parent: did you practice saying them together?

title: Two Truths and a Strength
summary: A group icebreaker where each person shares two true strengths and one exaggerated one for others to guess.
goal: Use it to get a group naming their own strengths out loud in a low-pressure, playful format.
body_md: Each player shares three statements about their own strengths, two true and one exaggerated, and the group guesses which is the stretch. Naming strengths about oneself can feel uncomfortable for a group working on self-esteem, and the playful framing lowers that discomfort enough that most people can do it without much hesitation. Debrief what it felt like to claim a strength out loud.

fields.label: Your two true strengths
Your one exaggerated strength
What did the group guess, and did they get it right?
What was it like to say a real strength about yourself?

title: Social Safety Behaviors Checklist
summary: Lists the subtle safety behaviors a client uses in social situations, as targets to gradually drop.
goal: Use it to name the small self-protective habits that quietly keep social anxiety in place.
body_md: Safety behaviors in social anxiety are often subtle enough to go unnoticed — rehearsing a line beforehand, avoiding eye contact, over-explaining, gripping a drink to look occupied. Each one feels protective but also prevents the client from learning the situation would have gone fine without it. The client lists their own behaviors and picks one to drop, on purpose, in a low-stakes situation first.

fields.label: Safety behaviors you use in social situations
Which one feels hardest to drop?
Pick one low-stakes situation to try dropping it
What happened when you dropped it?

title: Spotlight Effect Check
summary: Tests the belief that others notice a client’s mistakes or anxiety as much as it feels like they do.
goal: Use it to gather evidence against the assumption that everyone is watching as closely as it feels.
body_md: Social anxiety tends to inflate how much other people are actually noticing — a mistake that feels glaring to the person who made it is often missed entirely by everyone else, who are usually thinking about themselves. The client predicts how many people will notice a small slip before a situation, then checks afterward what evidence there actually was that anyone did.

fields.label: The situation and the slip you are worried about
Prediction: how many people will notice?
What actually happened — any evidence anyone noticed?
What does the gap between prediction and evidence tell you?

title: GIVE Skills Social Practice Card
summary: Adapts the DBT GIVE skill into a short script for practicing one low-stakes social interaction at a time.
goal: Use it to pair an interpersonal skill with graded social exposure instead of avoiding the interaction entirely.
body_md: GIVE, being gentle, showing interest, validating, and using an easy manner, gives a client something concrete to focus on that is not their own anxiety symptoms. The card pairs one GIVE element with a specific low-stakes interaction to try this week, shifting attention outward onto the skill rather than inward onto self-monitoring, which tends to fuel the anxiety further.

fields.label: The low-stakes interaction you will practice
Which GIVE element will you focus on?
What did you notice about your anxiety during it?
How did focusing on the skill change where your attention went?

title: One New Hello Chart
summary: A daily chart where a child tracks saying hello to just one person, building social approach one small step at a time.
goal: Use it to build social approach skill gradually, starting from the smallest possible step.
body_md: For a socially anxious child, a whole conversation can feel out of reach, but saying one hello usually does not. The chart tracks just that, one hello to one person a day, checked off with a sticker, without any pressure for the interaction to go further. Small, repeated wins build a track record the child can point to, which matters more than any single successful conversation.

fields.label: Who did you say hello to today?
What did that feel like before you did it?
What did it feel like after?
Parent: sticker earned — yes or no?

title: Icebreaker Ladder Game
summary: A group game climbing from very low-stakes to slightly harder icebreaker questions, one rung at a time.
goal: Use it to practice graded social exposure inside a group in a structured, predictable format.
body_md: Questions start as low-stakes as possible, a favorite color, a favorite food, and climb gradually toward slightly more personal ones as the group warms up, giving socially anxious members a predictable, low-pressure ramp instead of an unpredictable jump straight into deep sharing. Anyone can pass on a rung and try it again later, which keeps the exposure graded rather than forced.

fields.label: Which rung did you find hardest?
Did you pass on any question, and try it again later?
What helped you answer as the questions got more personal?
What did you notice about the group as the game went on?

title: Grief Anniversary Planning Sheet
summary: Plans ahead for an anniversary, holiday or other date that tends to bring grief back to the surface.
goal: Use it so a hard date is met with a plan instead of arriving unprepared.
body_md: Anniversaries, birthdays and holidays after a loss often hit harder than expected, even when the date has been circled on the calendar for weeks. The client plans ahead of time what they want the day to include — a ritual, time alone, company, avoiding a particular place — rather than deciding in the moment when grief may already be running the day.

fields.label: The upcoming date and what it marks
What do you want this day to include?
What do you want to avoid on this day?
Who, if anyone, do you want with you?

title: Grief Guilt Thought Record
summary: A thought record built around the guilt thoughts that often follow a loss, tested the same as any other.
goal: Use it to examine grief-related guilt thoughts with the same rigor as any other automatic thought.
body_md: ‘I should have called more’ or ‘I could have caught it sooner’ are common after a loss and rarely get examined the way an anxious thought would, because guilt can feel like proof of love rather than a thought worth questioning. The client logs the guilt thought, the evidence for and against it, and a more balanced version, treating it as a thought like any other.

fields.label: The guilt thought
Evidence that supports it
Evidence against it
A more balanced version of the thought

title: Carrying It Forward Practice
summary: An acceptance practice for carrying grief forward alongside continued values-based living, not instead of it.
goal: Use it to counter the belief that moving toward life again means leaving grief, or the person, behind.
body_md: Grief and continuing to live do not have to trade off against each other, though it can feel that way, as if enjoying something again is a kind of forgetting. The client practices naming both at once: the loss that is still carried, and one values-based action taken anyway, in the same breath. The aim is not resolution but making room for both to be true together.

fields.label: What are you still carrying from this loss?
A value that still matters to you
One action in that direction you could take, carrying the loss with you
What comes up when you imagine doing both at once?

title: Grieving Differently Together Sheet
summary: Helps a couple grieving the same loss understand why they are grieving in different ways and on different timelines.
goal: Use it to stop divergent grieving styles from being read as one partner caring less.
body_md: Two people grieving the same loss rarely grieve identically — one partner may want to talk often, the other may need quiet or activity, and each can misread the other’s style as not caring enough. Each partner describes their own grieving style and what they need from the other, and both name one thing they can stop assuming about the other’s grief once they hear this.

fields.label: Partner A: how does your grief usually show up?
Partner A: what do you need from your partner right now?
Partner B: how does your grief usually show up?
Partner B: what do you need from your partner right now?
One assumption about each other’s grief you are ready to drop

title: Feelings About Goodbye Storybook Craft
summary: A child makes a simple illustrated booklet about their loss, in their own words and pictures, with a parent nearby.
goal: Use it to give a child a concrete, contained way to tell their own story about the loss, at their own pace.
body_md: Children often process loss in pieces rather than one conversation, and a small illustrated booklet gives them somewhere to put those pieces over time rather than needing to say everything at once. The parent stays nearby to help with words but lets the child lead the pictures and the pace, adding pages over days or weeks rather than finishing in one sitting.

fields.label: What happened, in your own words or pictures
What you miss most
A happy memory to include
Who helps you when you feel sad about it

title: Relationship Pattern History Sheet
summary: Has a client trace a recurring relationship pattern across several relationships, not just the current one.
goal: Use it to show a client a pattern is theirs to work on, not just a feature of one difficult partner.
body_md: A pattern that shows up across several relationships, always the one who chases, always drawn to someone unavailable, always the one who goes quiet first, is more useful to examine than one blamed entirely on the current partner. The client lists past and current relationships and marks where the pattern shows up in each, then considers what role they tend to play in keeping it going.

fields.label: The pattern you keep noticing
Where did it show up in past relationships?
Where does it show up now?
What is your part in keeping the pattern going?

title: Mind-Reading Check for Relationships
summary: Tests an assumption about a partner’s thoughts or intentions against what they actually said when asked.
goal: Use it to interrupt the habit of assuming a partner’s intent instead of checking it directly.
body_md: ‘They didn’t text back because they’re losing interest’ is a guess dressed up as a fact, and relationships absorb a lot of friction from guesses like it going unchecked. The client writes the assumption, rates how certain they feel, then actually asks the partner and logs the real answer. Comparing the guess to the answer over a few entries usually reveals how often the guess was simply wrong.

fields.label: The assumption about your partner’s thoughts or intent
How certain did you feel, 0 to 100 percent?
What did they actually say when you asked?
How far off was the assumption?

title: Committed Relationship Values Check
summary: Practices willingness to sit with discomfort, an awkward conversation, being vulnerable, in service of the relationship.
goal: Use it when avoiding discomfort is quietly costing a client the relationship closeness they say they want.
body_md: Avoiding an awkward conversation or staying guarded to sidestep discomfort often costs more closeness than the discomfort itself would have. The client names a relationship value, honesty, closeness, repair, and one uncomfortable action that would actually serve it, then practices willingness to feel the discomfort rather than waiting for it to go away first.

fields.label: A relationship value that matters to you
What uncomfortable action would actually serve it?
What discomfort shows up when you imagine doing it?
Are you willing to feel that, in service of the value?

title: Relationship Check the Facts Sheet
summary: Applies DBT’s check the facts skill to a relationship conflict interpretation before reacting to it.
goal: Use it to test whether a reaction to a partner’s words actually fits the facts of what was said.
body_md: An emotional reaction to a partner’s comment sometimes fits the facts and sometimes runs ahead of them, shaped by past hurts more than the present moment. The client writes exactly what was said, their interpretation of it, and the emotion that followed, then checks whether the interpretation is the only one that fits the actual words. Where it does not, a different response usually becomes available.

fields.label: What was actually said, word for word if possible
Your interpretation of it
The emotion that followed, and its intensity
Is your interpretation the only one that fits the facts?

title: Repeated Argument Autopsy
summary: Has a couple analyze the structure of a recurring argument, how it starts, escalates and ends, rather than its content.
goal: Use it to interrupt a recurring argument’s pattern once both partners can see its shape.
body_md: The same argument often repeats not because the topic keeps changing but because the structure never does, a familiar opening line, a predictable escalation, the same ending. Each partner separately describes the pattern’s stages, then the two compare notes and name the exact moment where a different move could change the outcome. Working on the structure tends to help more than re-litigating the last instance.

fields.label: Partner A: how does this argument usually start?
Partner B: how does this argument usually start?
How does it usually escalate, and how does it usually end?
Where is the one moment a different move could change it?

title: Safety Signal Card
summary: A card naming a client’s own signals of safety in the present, built for quick reference during distress.
goal: Use it to give a client something concrete pointing to present safety, ready before it is needed.
body_md: Built on a calm day, the card lists specific, personal signals that the present is safe — a locked door, a trusted person’s number, a phrase that has worked before. It does not ask for any account of what happened; it works entirely in the present tense. If distress escalates toward a crisis, 988 (call or text) and the client’s own safety plan come next, not this card alone.

fields.label: A place that feels safe to you right now
A person you can reach out to
A phrase or reminder that has helped before
Where will you keep this card?

title: Self-Blame Versus Responsibility Sheet
summary: Separates a client’s self-blame from where responsibility actually sits, without needing the details of what happened.
goal: Use it to loosen self-blame that has settled somewhere it does not belong.
body_md: Self-blame after sexual abuse often attaches to choices the client made, what they wore, where they were, what they said, as though those choices caused the abuse. The client can name the self-blaming thought and test it against a simple question: who chose to cause harm? The exercise works without any account of the abuse itself; it stays with the thought, not the story.

fields.label: A self-blaming thought you carry
What choice does it blame you for?
Who actually chose to cause harm?
What would you say to someone else carrying this same blame?

title: Reclaiming Choice Practice
summary: Practices noticing small present-day choices a client has, to rebuild a sense of agency at their own pace.
goal: Use it to rebuild a felt sense of choice in the present, without needing to revisit the past.
body_md: Abuse involves choice being taken away, and rebuilding a felt sense of agency can matter as much as any other part of healing, entirely apart from processing what happened. The practice has the client notice small, real choices available right now, what to eat, when to rest, who to see, and name each one as evidence that choice is theirs again. No account of the abuse itself is needed for this to work.

fields.label: A small choice you made today
How did it feel to notice it as your choice?
What is one more choice available to you this week?
What does having choice again mean to you?

title: Body Safety Grounding Card
summary: A grounding sequence for the body-based distress that can follow sexual abuse, without revisiting any details.
goal: Use it to bring the body back to a felt sense of safety when distress spikes.
body_md: Distress after sexual abuse can show up first in the body, tension, disconnection, a racing heart, before any thought is even named. The card walks through a short, body-based grounding sequence: feet on the floor, hands on a solid surface, a slow count of the breath. It works without any narrative content and can be practiced calm, in session, before it is needed elsewhere.

fields.label: Where do you notice the distress in your body first?
Feet on the floor — what do you notice?
Hands on a solid surface — what do you notice?
Rate the distress before and after this sequence

title: Trusted Grown-Ups Map
summary: A child maps the trusted grown-ups they could go to if something felt wrong or unsafe.
goal: Use it to build a child’s concrete list of safe adults to turn to, before it is ever needed.
body_md: The child draws or names a small circle of trusted grown-ups, at home, at school, in the family, they could go to if something ever felt wrong or unsafe, without needing to describe any specific worry to complete the map. Clinician note: if a child discloses anything during this or any session, follow your setting’s mandated reporting duties promptly, before continuing any other work.

fields.label: Draw or name your trusted grown-ups
How could you find each one if you needed to?
What could you say to a grown-up if something felt wrong?
Parent or caregiver: is this map somewhere the child can remember it?

title: Coping Skills Audit by Situation
summary: Sorts a client’s coping skills by which situations they actually work best in, rather than one skill for all.
goal: Use it to match a coping skill to the situation instead of reaching for the same one every time.
body_md: A skill that works well for a racing mind at 2am may do nothing for a tense conversation at work, and clients often keep reaching for the same familiar skill regardless of fit. The client sorts their current coping skills by situation type, physical activation, racing thoughts, interpersonal conflict, low energy, building a reference to pull from instead of one default.

fields.label: Skills that help with physical activation (racing heart, tension)
Skills that help with racing or looping thoughts
Skills that help in interpersonal conflict
Skills that help on low-energy days
Which situation type do you have the fewest skills for?

title: Workable Coping Sort
summary: Sorts coping behaviors into those that move a client toward their values and those that only move away from pain.
goal: Use it to notice which coping strategies build a life a client wants, not just relieve a moment.
body_md: Two coping behaviors can both bring short-term relief while pointing in opposite directions, one toward a life the client actually wants, the other only away from discomfort with nothing gained. The client sorts a list of their current coping behaviors into these two columns and looks at which column they reach for most, then considers where one ‘away from’ behavior could shift toward a ‘toward’ one.

fields.label: Coping behaviors that move you toward something you value
Coping behaviors that only move you away from discomfort
Which column do you reach for most?
One ‘away from’ behavior you could shift toward a value

title: Skills Chain Backup Plan
summary: Plans a second and third coping skill in advance, in case the first choice does not work in the moment.
goal: Use it so a client has a next move ready instead of stalling when the first skill falls short.
body_md: A single coping plan can leave a client stuck if the first skill they reach for does not work in the moment, which can feel like the whole plan failing rather than one option not fitting. The client plans a short chain, first skill, then a backup, then a third, ahead of time, so there is always a next move ready rather than starting from scratch mid-distress.

fields.label: Your first-choice skill for this kind of moment
Backup skill if the first one does not work
Third option if neither works
Which one did you actually end up using, and how far down the chain?

title: Calm-Down Card Deck Craft
summary: A child illustrates a small deck of cards, one coping skill per card, to shuffle through when upset.
goal: Use it to give a child a hands-on deck of options they made themselves and can physically shuffle through.
body_md: The child draws one coping skill per card, blowing bubbles, squeezing a pillow, counting to ten, asking for a hug, building a small deck over several sessions. When upset, the child (or parent, at first) shuffles through the deck to pick one to try, which turns ‘use a coping skill’ into a concrete, game-like action instead of an abstract instruction to remember.

fields.label: What coping skill is on today’s new card?
Draw a picture for it
Which card did you pick the last time you were upset?
Did it help? Parent: what did you notice?

title: Skill or Bluff
summary: A guessing game where players describe a coping skill, real or invented, and the group votes on which it is.
goal: Use it to review real coping skills while keeping the format playful and a little competitive.
body_md: Each player describes a coping skill with a straight face, some real, some invented on the spot, and the group votes on whether it is genuine or a bluff, earning a point for a correct guess either way. The debrief sorts out which described skills were real and worth remembering, folding review into a game that plays more like a party game than a therapy exercise.

fields.label: The skill you described — real or a bluff?
Did the group guess correctly?
Which real skills came up that you want to remember?
Which bluff skill was the funniest?

title: Safe Zone Shrinking Map
summary: Maps how a client’s everyday ‘safe zone’ of places and activities has shrunk as a specific fear grew.
goal: Use it to show a client how much territory avoidance has quietly claimed, and pick one edge to push back.
body_md: A specific phobia tends to expand its no-go zone gradually enough that a client stops noticing how much has been given up, avoiding driving on highways can end up limiting a job search; avoiding dogs can end up limiting which friends’ homes get visited. The client draws their current safe zone against what it used to include, then picks one edge of the shrunken territory to reclaim first.

fields.label: What does your safe zone include today?
What did it used to include before the fear grew?
Which edge of the shrunken zone matters most to reclaim?
What would the first small step back into it look like?

title: Feared Outcome Likelihood Sheet
summary: Has a client estimate the real-world odds of their feared outcome, then compares it to base rates.
goal: Use it to put a number on a feared outcome instead of letting it stay an unexamined certainty.
body_md: A specific phobia often runs on an outcome that feels certain but is, in fact, rare, the plane will crash, the dog will bite, the elevator will get stuck. The client estimates their own odds, then the two of you look together at what is actually known about the base rate for that outcome. The gap between the felt certainty and the real odds becomes something concrete to work with.

fields.label: The feared outcome
Your estimate of the odds it happens, in percent
What is actually known about the real odds?
How does that gap change how certain the fear feels?

title: Fear Passenger Exposure Log
summary: Logs approach steps toward a feared object or situation with fear allowed to come along, not required to leave first.
goal: Use it to decouple doing the approach step from feeling calm enough to do it first.
body_md: Waiting to feel calm before approaching a feared situation usually means waiting indefinitely, since the calm tends to arrive after repeated approach, not before it. The client logs each approach step alongside how much fear was present and whether they did the step anyway, treating the fear as an unwelcome passenger rather than a stop sign.

fields.label: Today’s approach step
Fear level going in, 0 to 10
Did you do the step with the fear present?
What did the fear do during and after the step?

title: Fear Ladder Sticker Chart
summary: A sticker chart tracking a child’s steps up their own fear ladder, one small approach step at a time.
goal: Use it to make gradual progress up a fear ladder visible and rewarding for a child.
body_md: Built together with the parent, the ladder breaks a specific fear into small graded steps, and each completed step earns a sticker on the chart. Progress up a fear ladder can feel invisible day to day, and the chart gives the child something to look back at and see how far they have actually climbed. Celebrate effort at each step, not only reaching the top.

fields.label: Your fear ladder, from easiest to hardest step
Which step did you try today?
How scared were you before, and after?
Parent: sticker earned — yes or no?

title: Fear Facts Quiz Show
summary: A quiz game that corrects common myths about feared objects and situations, in a playful group format.
goal: Use it to chip away at threat overestimation with real information, delivered as a game rather than a lecture.
body_md: Questions test common beliefs about feared things, how likely a dog is to bite, how safe air travel actually is, how elevators are inspected, and players guess true or false before hearing the real answer. Presenting accurate information as a game rather than a lecture tends to land better with a group that already feels defensive about being told their fear is irrational.

fields.label: Which question surprised you the most?
What did you believe before, and what is actually true?
Does this change how big the fear feels?
What is one question you would add to the quiz?

title: Body Talk Audit
summary: Tracks how often a client’s day includes appearance-focused talk or comparison, in conversation or media.
goal: Use it to make an often-invisible daily habit of appearance talk visible and open to change.
body_md: Appearance-focused comments, from others, in media, or self-directed, can run through a day almost unnoticed until they are tracked on purpose. The client logs each instance along with how it affected their mood, then looks for patterns: certain people, certain apps, certain times of day. The goal is awareness first; specific changes come once the pattern is visible.

fields.label: The appearance-focused moment (conversation, media, self-talk)
Where did it come from?
How did it affect your mood?
What pattern are you noticing across entries?

title: Appearance Comparison Interrupt Sheet
summary: Catches an automatic appearance comparison and tests the assumption behind it before it settles in.
goal: Use it to interrupt an automatic comparison before it turns into a settled negative belief.
body_md: A comparison, to a photo, a stranger, a past version of oneself, often happens in a split second and gets treated as a verdict rather than a passing thought. The client catches the comparison, writes the assumption behind it, and asks what is actually known instead of assumed. Slowing the moment down tends to loosen its grip more than trying to avoid comparisons altogether.

fields.label: The comparison that came up
What assumption is behind it?
What do you actually know, versus assume?
What would you say to a friend having this same comparison?

title: Body as Vehicle Practice
summary: Shifts attention from how the body looks to what it allows a client to do in service of their values.
goal: Use it to widen a client’s relationship with their body beyond appearance alone.
body_md: The body carries a person toward the things they value, a walk with a friend, picking up a child, standing at a job that matters, regardless of how it looks doing it. The client names a recent moment the body made a valued activity possible and practices noticing that function, not appearance, as what the moment was actually about. Repetition matters more than any single entry here.

fields.label: A recent moment your body made something you value possible
What did your body let you do in that moment?
What would you have missed without it?
What does thanking your body for function, not appearance, feel like?

title: Body Image Opposite Action Card
summary: Applies the DBT opposite action skill to the urge to avoid or hide that body image distress often brings.
goal: Use it to interrupt avoidance driven by body image distress before it narrows a client’s life further.
body_md: Body image distress often comes with an urge to avoid, skip the event, cancel the photo, stay home, that can quietly shrink a client’s life over time if it goes unexamined. The client names the urge, checks whether acting on it fits the actual situation, and practices the opposite action fully when it does not, going to the event rather than only partly showing up.

fields.label: The situation and the urge to avoid or hide
Does the urge fit the actual situation?
The opposite action, described fully
What happened when you did the opposite action?

title: Body Image Support Conversation Guide
summary: Helps a partner learn to support body image struggles without appearance-focused comments that can backfire.
goal: Use it to replace well-meaning appearance comments with support that actually helps.
body_md: A partner’s well-meant reassurance about appearance can land badly for someone struggling with body image, since it keeps the conversation centered on looks either way. The guide has the struggling partner describe what kind of support actually helps, distraction, a hug, a change of subject, and the other partner practices offering that instead of a compliment about appearance.

fields.label: Struggling partner: what kind of support actually helps you?
Struggling partner: what comments, even kind ones, make it worse?
Supporting partner: what will you try saying or doing instead?
How did it go the last time you tried this?
